title: A Sleep Scientist Explains Why Exhaustion Doesn't Guarantee Sleep
script: Host: [thoughtful] Welcome back. Today we're exploring something almost everyone struggles with occasionally: falling asleep despite feeling genuinely exhausted. Thanks for joining us, Dr. Chandra.
Dr. Chandra: Thank you for having me. It's a paradox that confuses more people than you'd expect, exhaustion without the ability to actually sleep.
Host: [carefully] Why does that happen? Shouldn't tiredness guarantee sleep almost automatically?
Dr. Chandra: You'd assume so, but sleep depends on more than fatigue alone; it depends heavily on your circadian rhythm being properly aligned.
Host: [reflective] Can you explain what throws that rhythm off for most people, beyond the obvious culprit of staring at phones?
Dr. Chandra: Inconsistent wake times matter more than people realize. Sleeping in on weekends essentially recreates jet lag without ever leaving your city.
Host: [honestly] That's a striking comparison. So the damage isn't only from going to bed late, but from waking up inconsistently?
Dr. Chandra: Precisely. Your body relies on a predictable signal each morning to regulate hormones that eventually make you sleepy again at night.
Host: [gently] What about people who insist caffeine has no effect on them, even when consumed late in the afternoon?
Dr. Chandra: That belief is remarkably common and remarkably mistaken. Caffeine can linger in your system for hours longer than most people assume.
Host: [calmly] So someone might fall asleep fine, yet still be experiencing disrupted sleep without realizing caffeine is the cause?
Dr. Chandra: Exactly right. The disruption often shows up as lighter, more fragmented sleep rather than difficulty falling asleep itself.
Host: [encouraging] What would you say to listeners who've tried everything, dark rooms, no screens, and still struggle most nights?
Dr. Chandra: I'd ask whether anxiety about sleep itself has become the actual obstacle, which happens more often than people expect.
Host: [seriously] Meaning the worry about not sleeping becomes its own barrier to sleeping?
Dr. Chandra: Precisely that. Lying awake calculating remaining hours only heightens the alertness you're desperately trying to escape.
Host: That's a frustrating cycle. Any practical advice for someone caught inside it right now?
Dr. Chandra: If sleep hasn't arrived within twenty minutes, get up briefly rather than lying there battling it, then return once genuinely drowsy.
